findings.passage: The strongest Four evidence is recent and unprompted. Describing that collapse to Sharpe, he said what he had wanted from the people around him: "People should be telling me it's going to be okay. People should be trying to help me." Then he described his own habit of mind as "my problems, my music, I'm sad, my this, my that," and compared himself to a character who thinks the world revolves around her.
findings.problem: Editor-introduced context distortion in suicide-adjacent testimony. Club Shay Shay auto transcript, re-pulled 2026-09-18, ~101:45-108:10: Sharpe asks whether Rod missed signs before Lil Poppa's suicide, and these lines are part of that answer. Rod brings up the Fault in Our Stars character to make the point that 'it's not this about me... Everybody going through something'. He then says he felt people should be telling him it would be okay, and adds 'that situation really woke me up... you got to check on your strong friends'. 'my problems, my music, I'm sad, my this, my that' comes after 'could I have done better, dog?' about Poppa. The article presents a self-criticism he says he outgrew as his current 'habit of mind', calls it 'unprompted', and makes it the strongest Four evidence. It drops the fact that in the same breath he corrects himself toward the ordinary, which is the article's own leading Nine discriminator. The editor added this material at edit stage (C92), taken from the same passage that subject-01, fan-06 and critic-09 flagged. No reviewer has seen this framing. The Type 4 FAQ (C80) repeats it.
findings.acceptance_test: Body and Type 4 FAQ present the lines as a retrospective self-criticism: while the tour was falling apart he was absorbed in his own problems, and he says the period 'woke me up' to the fact that 'everybody going through something'. No death needs to be named, but the text no longer calls it 'unprompted' or a present 'habit of mind'. The article says whether the self-correction counts for the Four reading, the Nine reading or neither. C92 and C80 record the question he was answering and the ~104:00-108:10 locator. This is new edit-stage use of suicide-adjacent material, so the repaired passage goes to the expanded jury before release.

findings.passage: Then he was gone for nineteen months, and _Don't Look Down_ arrived in August 2026 and debuted at No. 1 with 99,000 equivalent album units. One rebuke and a long exit is the pattern, not an absence of grievance.
findings.problem: Nineteen months is the gap between albums, not an absence, and the packet's own sources say so. Wikipedia (S16) records the 'Sinners' single in April 2025, three months after the hiatus post. Rolling Stone (S14) reports it earned his first Grammy nomination. Billboard (S06, September 8, 2025) reports a sold-out hometown arena show in Tampa on August 29, 2025. Mainstay launched in 2025, and the countersuit coverage (S10) announces his Redemption Experience tour. The article itself mentions Mainstay, the September 2025 interview and the 'Sinners' nomination. The claim does argumentative work in three places: the Type 8 discriminator ('The January 2025 criticism produced one rebuke and a nineteen-month absence'), the pattern claim quoted above, and 'the long quiet that followed it' in the closing. None of these three statements about absence is inventoried as a claim.
findings.acceptance_test: Every mention describes the gap accurately: nineteen months between albums, with the April 2025 single, the 2025 Mainstay launch and the August 2025 return to the stage dated. The exit-rather-than-argument reading is re-weighed against a step back of months, not a year and a half. 'The long quiet' is corrected. The absence claim is inventoried with S06/S16 support.

findings.problem: This mischaracterizes a pending criminal case. The LA Times (S13, May 21, 2025), which the article cites, reports the May 2025 Fulton County booking on 14 charges, including aggravated and simple assault and 'pointing or aiming a gun or pistol at another'. Rolling Stone (S14, November 10, 2025) recaps them as aggravated assault, aiming a gun at someone, simple assault and battery. At least three adult cases allege violence, not two. For the May case the article prints only the defense's account ('a victim of a burglary') and then says 'Neither alleges anger.' That treats one side's framing of a disputed matter as fact. Neither sentence is in the evidence inventory.
findings.acceptance_test: The May 2025 case names the nature of the charges neutrally (for example 'charged with aggravated assault and other counts from an April 2025 incident') beside his lawyers' denial and the absence of any reported disposition. The count of violence-alleging adult cases is corrected or removed. 'Neither alleges anger' is limited to the November drug and weapons case or deleted. The section still draws no personality inference from any charge. The corrected sentences are inventoried with S13/S14 and an unresolved review_trigger.

findings.passage: The second discriminator is the shape of his fights, and it is aimed at Type 8. He fights often, but never face to face.
findings.problem: The discriminator against Type 8 is stated as an absolute no source can establish, and the article's own later sections complicate it. The temper section reports a promoter's claim that Rod hit him after the 2020 stage collapse, the 2022 domestic battery charge, and the May 2025 assault case (see verify-03). It also quotes his own account of expressing adolescent anger 'in dangerous' ways. The article is right not to treat unproven allegations as evidence, but the same rule stops it asserting the opposite. The record supports something narrower: his documented disputes with his label, his promoter and his critics ran through a post, a filing and an exit. As written, the Nine-over-Eight case claims more than the evidence shows.
findings.acceptance_test: The claim is limited to the documented business and public disputes. The article says the untested physical-confrontation allegations count neither way. With verify-02 corrected, the paragraph no longer relies on a nineteen-month absence. C99's inference and alternative state the limit. If the narrowed discriminator no longer separates 9 from 8, the type section, FAQ and type_hypothesis say so.

findings.passage: It alleges that Grizzly failed to "properly load his touring equipment in and out of the venues" and made "unilateral, onerous and inexplicable routing and booking decisions"
findings.problem: A court filing is misquoted in the sensitive-allegations section. Billboard Pro (S10, October 13, 2025) gives the load-in claim as its own unquoted paraphrase, 'failing to properly load his touring equipment in and out of arenas'. The article puts it in quotation marks as the countersuit's words and changes 'arenas' to 'venues'. The same Billboard piece reports the countersuit's statement that the alleged $1.8 million scheme 'was unsuccessful ... as Rod identified and rejected this exclusivity language'. The article omits this, leaving readers to assume a clause was slipped into his contract. That changes how an allegation against a named third party, Beau Williams, reads.
findings.acceptance_test: The load-in allegation is given as Billboard's summary, without quotation marks, or with Billboard's exact wording. Only the source's own quoted phrases stay in quotation marks. The Williams sentence adds that the countersuit says the attempt failed because he rejected the clause. C36's passage and inference are updated.

findings.problem: Several quotations drift from their sources. (1) Club Shay Shay ~6:20 reads 'it might be a 50/50 problem'; 'maybe' is not in the quoted phrase. (2) Breakfast Club ~7:10 reads 'I give them so so little that they got to use they got to work with what they got'; the quotation removes a repetition and a false start without marking them. (3) Club Shay Shay ~26:05 reads 'I'm stoked with the aftermath of what you guys ruined'. 'stuck' is a plausible fix for an auto-transcript error ('I'm stuck cleaning up what y'all messed up' follows), but it is unmarked. (4) DJ Smallz Eyes 2018 ~23:07 answers 'any regrets' with 'I regret stealing from innocent people'; 'deepest regret' adds a superlative. (5) Billboard 2023 says his father put him in football 'when I got out of jail', meaning his own juvenile detention; 'who put him into football after prison' says prison and is ambiguous about whose.
findings.acceptance_test: (1) is quoted as 'a 50/50 problem' or 'it might be a 50/50 problem'. (2) and (3) are confirmed against the audio, or the changes are marked. (4) says he named it as his regret. (5) says after his stint in juvenile detention, or quotes Billboard.

findings.passage: He flattens it, and he was doing it before there was an album to sell.
findings.problem: The 2020 Complex interview behind this sentence ran on April 3, 2020, the release day of Pray 4 Love, and Complex frames it around that album. There was an album to sell. What the argument needs, and what the next paragraph states correctly, is that in 2020 he had 'no reputation for calm to protect' and no growth-themed album to promote.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence says what the 2020 material predates (the calmer-man album cycle and any reputation for calm), not that no album was being promoted.

findings.passage: Lane died in July 2024, seven months before the Last Lap tour fell apart, and no cause of death has been publicly released
findings.problem: Revolt/Rap-Up (S20, July 3, 2024) says only that no cause had been revealed 'at the time of reporting'. On Club Shay Shay (August 26, 2026, ~105:02) Rod himself said his uncle 'passed away the same way' as Lil Poppa, while also saying he could not believe it. As a present-tense statement in September 2026, 'no cause of death has been publicly released' is inaccurate. The editor was right not to repeat Rod's remark.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence says no official cause of death has been released, or that Revolt reported at the time that no cause had been revealed. It adds no remark about the manner of death. C87 notes the S01 remark and why it is not used.

findings.passage: He sounded similarly settled to Billboard in September 2025, three weeks before Grizzly Touring's suit made the dispute public.
findings.problem: The dispute was already public. Billboard's September 8, 2025 introduction reports that the tour was cancelled 'due to production and routing issues'. In the same interview he blamed 'the routing', and Grizzly's complaint cites that interview as public blame (S06 context). What the suit made public was the litigation, not the dispute.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence reads 'three weeks before Grizzly Touring sued him' or equivalent, and C78 is updated.

enneagram.reason: The argument is unusually honest. It concedes that circumstance explains his distance about as well as any type, tests 4 and 8 by name, and downgrades the image, peace and awards answers rather than padding the case. The leading discriminator, flattening a flattering frame in 2020, 2025 and 2026, is specific and dated. But it rests on things he says about himself in interviews, not repeated costly choices, and the article itself shows that the one costly test (awards) fails. The case against Type 8 leans on 'never face to face' and a 'nineteen-month absence', both overstated (verify-04, verify-02). It also has to coexist with a drive for control and to prove a point, which the article admits Nine theory does not explain. The Type 4 alternative is argued seriously, but its best new evidence is misframed (verify-01). Medium confidence is the right call. It does not yet reach the 8 anchor, where the strongest alternative fails a specific, sourced discriminator.
